actions.title: SAGE Shared-Responsibility, Governed Orchestration, and Outcome Metamodel
actions.desired_outcome: SAGE has an explicit implementation-neutral shared-responsibility, governed-orchestration, verification, observability, and outcome metamodel for evidence-informed intent-to-outcome system engineering. Human participants provide legitimate intent and accountable authority; the LLM is a first-class contributor of external/world knowledge, alternatives, critique, and verification ideas without human-reserved approval authority; Kalaxy3 provides accumulated local evidence, experience, standards, and measured outcomes; and deterministic orchestration owns reproducible workflow state, transitions, retry, compensation, and continuation. SAGE federates and reconciles those participant contributions under cross-cutting governance, verification/assurance, observability, and continuous improvement. The human Architect role retains end-to-end accountable architectural ownership and a governed, attributable break-glass path that can regain architectural control without making the intervention unaccountable. Success is evaluated first by mandatory outcome gates and then by a provenance-preserving multidimensional outcome vector against human-owned intent, requirements, constraints, and Definition of Done; any scalar fitness or utility function is optional, context-specific, and human-owned/approved. The metamodel remains implementation-neutral and does not prematurely select BPMN, a workflow engine, graph technology, or another orchestration product.
acceptance_criteria: The metamodel defines four first-class participant classes: human participants, LLM, Kalaxy3 evidence/experience, and deterministic orchestration/execution, with SAGE defined as the governing system-engineering federation that reconciles their inputs into governed decisions.

Human participant roles include stakeholder/sponsor/product owner, architect/engineer, operator, and reviewer/approver; the same human may hold multiple roles, and authority is represented as an explicit governed property rather than inferred from technical capability.

Shared-responsibility vocabulary defines Accountable Owner, Responsible, Contributor, Authority-Approver, and optional Informed responsibilities per activity; capability overlap is allowed while accountability and legitimate authority remain explicit.

The human Architect role has end-to-end accountable architectural responsibility for intended future state, requirements, constraints, Definition of Done, approval boundaries, and architectural fitness; multiple qualified humans may hold the role, but nothing inside SAGE can make the Architect unable to regain architectural control.

Architect break-glass intervention is exceptional, explicit, minimum-scope, attributable, and records trigger, rationale, controls or assumptions overridden, resulting risk, and required post-verification; it cannot nullify external legal, security, compliance, or other nondelegable constraints, and recurring intervention classes become continuous-improvement evidence.

The LLM is a first-class contributor of external/world knowledge, state-of-practice patterns, alternatives, critique, risk identification, and verification ideas, while remaining untrusted with authority: it cannot be the Accountable Architect, sole source of legitimate stakeholder intent, or holder of human-reserved approval authority.

Kalaxy3 is explicitly modeled as accumulated local evidence and experience, including current facts, validated lessons, standards, workflow experience, measurements, and reusable capability; SAGE reconciles this local experience with human intent, LLM knowledge, and current evidence.

Deterministic orchestration/execution owns reproducible workflow state, transitions, decisions, branches, retry, compensation, continuation, and exact mutation boundaries; LLM output may propose or inform these operations but does not own deterministic workflow state or transition authority.

Governance is cross-cutting across the lifecycle and covers intent, authority, provenance, evidence applicability/admissibility, mutation scope, capability selection, validation, approvals, promotion, completion, and evidence-backed disposition of unexpected inferred contexts.

Unexpected inferred contexts receive an explicit evidence-backed disposition of applicable-now, conceptually-applicable-but-not-currently-instrumented, capability-gap, or demonstrably-not-applicable; broader applicable contexts are not suppressed merely because the immediate implementation is narrower.

Verification/assurance spans the complete lifecycle rather than being a terminal box: humans contribute semantic correctness and judgment, LLMs contribute challenge and validation ideas that require corroboration, Kalaxy3 contributes facts and prior evidence, SAGE determines applicable checks and evidence sufficiency, deterministic primitives perform reproducible validation, and observability contributes measured evidence.

The lifecycle is explicitly represented as Intent -> Understanding -> Decision -> Execution -> Measurement/Learning -> Improved capability, with verification/assurance and governance spanning all stages.

Observability is a quantitative SAGE capability covering workflow and decision observability in addition to infrastructure/application observability, including effectiveness, efficiency, quality, friction, rework, failure recurrence, time to validated outcome, human intervention, prediction calibration, cost, reuse, outcome/system metrics, and optimization opportunities.

Continuous improvement consumes verified outcomes, observability, failures, interventions, evidence use, and validated paths to create or harden reusable repository-owned capability and to reduce recurrence, avoidable rework, and repeated governance reconstruction.

Result semantics use mandatory outcome gates for functional correctness, quality, safety/security/compliance, verification evidence, and prohibited side effects; failure of a mandatory gate cannot be averaged away by better performance on another dimension.

Beyond mandatory gates, SAGE preserves a provenance-backed multidimensional outcome vector against human-owned intent, requirements, constraints, and Definition of Done, including attainment, correctness/quality, reliability, time, human effort, cost, rework, recurrence, automation leverage, maintainability, stakeholder value, architectural fitness, and improvement opportunity where applicable.

A scalar fitness/utility score is used only when comparison or optimization requires it; its semantics, normalization, tradeoffs, and weights are explicitly human-owned and approved, SAGE/LLM may propose but may not invent the value function, and the underlying vector components and provenance remain available.

Anti-gaming controls prevent SAGE, an LLM, or an implementation from redefining success around convenient metrics, silently changing weights or gates, or substituting proxy optimization for the human-owned Definition of Done.

The metamodel is reconciled with the existing SAGE operating contract, workflow primitives, continuous-improvement model, evidence model, observability model, SAGE-ACTION-20260810-001, and SAGE-ACTION-20260809-002 without absorbing those actions' narrower implementation scopes.

An external-framework review is documented and published using authoritative current sources, covering relevant AWS, Microsoft Azure, IBM, Google Cloud, and NIST governance/architecture guidance; alignment is characterized as comparison, not certification or endorsement, and SAGE-specific extensions are explicitly identified.

Deterministic positive and negative regressions prove shared-responsibility authority boundaries, LLM non-authority, architect break-glass accountability, evidence-backed context disposition, mandatory-gate behavior, outcome-vector preservation, and human-owned scalar semantics.

No orchestration implementation product is selected by this action; BPMN, workflow engines, graph engines/databases, or other products remain later capability-selection decisions governed by measured requirements and evidence.
measurement_plan: Track activity-level responsibility assignments and authority boundaries, including Accountable Owner, Responsible, Contributor, Authority-Approver, and optional Informed roles, and record ambiguous or conflicting assignments as defects.

Track Architect interventions and break-glass events by trigger, rationale, minimum governed scope, controls or assumptions overridden, resulting risk, post-verification result, recurrence class, and whether the class becomes reusable capability.

Track LLM contributions by contribution type (external knowledge, alternatives, critique/risk, verification idea, candidate change), provenance, corroboration outcome, and whether any attempted use crossed a human-reserved or deterministic authority boundary.

Track inferred-context dispositions by applicable-now, conceptually-applicable-but-not-currently-instrumented, capability-gap, and demonstrably-not-applicable, with zero suppressions lacking evidence-backed disposition.

Track deterministic workflow decisions, transitions, retries, compensation, and continuations versus manual reconstruction, including failure recurrence, avoidable rework, and time to validated continuation.

Track workflow/decision observability coverage separately from infrastructure/application observability and measure missing instrumentation, human intervention, process friction, decision latency, and verification evidence availability.

For each governed outcome, record mandatory gate results independently and preserve the applicable multidimensional outcome vector with provenance; require zero cases where a failed mandatory gate is masked by aggregation.

Where a scalar fitness/utility score is used, record the human-approved value-function semantics, normalization, weights, tradeoffs, approval provenance, component vector, and sensitivity to changed assumptions; otherwise preserve scalar neutrality.

Measure effectiveness, efficiency, correctness/quality, reliability, time to validated outcome, human effort, cost, rework, recurrence, automation leverage, maintainability, stakeholder value, architectural fitness, prediction calibration, reuse, and improvement opportunity where the dimensions are applicable and observable.

Measure whether verified interventions, workflow outcomes, evidence use, failures, and repeated patterns are converted into reusable repository-owned capabilities that reduce recurrence, manual correction, governance reconstruction, and avoidable rework.

Record the external-framework review scope, authoritative source provenance, comparison date, identified alignments, deliberate SAGE-specific extensions, and unresolved gaps without treating comparison as certification or endorsement.

before_contract.title: Codify fit-for-purpose SAGE role and orchestration metamodel

acceptance_criteria: The SAGE operating contract explicitly defines the human architect as owner of intended future state, requirements, constraints, Definition of Done, approval boundaries, and explicit governed intervention when platform immaturity requires it.
Every architect intervention is required to be scoped, contextualized, justified, traceable, and observable rather than silently altering SAGE behavior or learned workflow assumptions.
SAGE is explicitly responsible for governing intent, applicability, authority, evidence, capability selection, progression, and disposition of unexpected inferred contexts.

LLMs are explicitly classified as untrusted stochastic proposers for exploration, interpretation, design, and candidate mutations and are prohibited from owning deterministic directed workflow state, transition authority, or graph traversal.

Unexpected inferred contexts cannot be suppressed merely because they are broader than the immediate implementation; each must receive an evidence-backed disposition such as applicable-now, conceptually-applicable-but-not-currently-instrumented, capability-gap, or demonstrably-not-applicable.

Workflow observability is distinguished from infrastructure observability so conceptually applicable workflow telemetry that is not yet instrumented is represented as an instrumentation or capability gap rather than a false-positive context.

The continuous-improvement model explicitly permits repeated architect interventions, workflow outcomes, evidence use, failures, and validated paths to be converted into reusable repository-owned workflow capability and measured for effectiveness, efficiency, recurrence, and avoidable rework.

The metamodel is reconciled with the existing SAGE operating contract, workflow primitives, continuous-improvement model, evidence model, observability model, SAGE-ACTION-20260810-001, and SAGE-ACTION-20260809-002 without absorbing those actions' narrower implementation scopes.

The metamodel remains implementation-neutral and does not prematurely select BPMN, a workflow engine, graph technology, or another orchestration product.
acceptance_criteria: The metamodel defines four first-class participant classes: human participants, LLM, Kalaxy3 evidence/experience, and deterministic orchestration/execution, with SAGE defined as the governing system-engineering federation that reconciles their inputs into governed decisions.

Human participant roles include stakeholder/sponsor/product owner, architect/engineer, operator, and reviewer/approver; the same human may hold multiple roles, and authority is represented as an explicit governed property rather than inferred from technical capability.

Shared-responsibility vocabulary defines Accountable Owner, Responsible, Contributor, Authority-Approver, and optional Informed responsibilities per activity; capability overlap is allowed while accountability and legitimate authority remain explicit.

The human Architect role has end-to-end accountable architectural responsibility for intended future state, requirements, constraints, Definition of Done, approval boundaries, and architectural fitness; multiple qualified humans may hold the role, but nothing inside SAGE can make the Architect unable to regain architectural control.

Architect break-glass intervention is exceptional, explicit, minimum-scope, attributable, and records trigger, rationale, controls or assumptions overridden, resulting risk, and required post-verification; it cannot nullify external legal, security, compliance, or other nondelegable constraints, and recurring intervention classes become continuous-improvement evidence.

The LLM is a first-class contributor of external/world knowledge, state-of-practice patterns, alternatives, critique, risk identification, and verification ideas, while remaining untrusted with authority: it cannot be the Accountable Architect, sole source of legitimate stakeholder intent, or holder of human-reserved approval authority.

Kalaxy3 is explicitly modeled as accumulated local evidence and experience, including current facts, validated lessons, standards, workflow experience, measurements, and reusable capability; SAGE reconciles this local experience with human intent, LLM knowledge, and current evidence.

Deterministic orchestration/execution owns reproducible workflow state, transitions, decisions, branches, retry, compensation, continuation, and exact mutation boundaries; LLM output may propose or inform these operations but does not own deterministic workflow state or transition authority.

Governance is cross-cutting across the lifecycle and covers intent, authority, provenance, evidence applicability/admissibility, mutation scope, capability selection, validation, approvals, promotion, completion, and evidence-backed disposition of unexpected inferred contexts.

Unexpected inferred contexts receive an explicit evidence-backed disposition of applicable-now, conceptually-applicable-but-not-currently-instrumented, capability-gap, or demonstrably-not-applicable; broader applicable contexts are not suppressed merely because the immediate implementation is narrower.

Verification/assurance spans the complete lifecycle rather than being a terminal box: humans contribute semantic correctness and judgment, LLMs contribute challenge and validation ideas that require corroboration, Kalaxy3 contributes facts and prior evidence, SAGE determines applicable checks and evidence sufficiency, deterministic primitives perform reproducible validation, and observability contributes measured evidence.

The lifecycle is explicitly represented as Intent -> Understanding -> Decision -> Execution -> Measurement/Learning -> Improved capability, with verification/assurance and governance spanning all stages.

Observability is a quantitative SAGE capability covering workflow and decision observability in addition to infrastructure/application observability, including effectiveness, efficiency, quality, friction, rework, failure recurrence, time to validated outcome, human intervention, prediction calibration, cost, reuse, outcome/system metrics, and optimization opportunities.

Continuous improvement consumes verified outcomes, observability, failures, interventions, evidence use, and validated paths to create or harden reusable repository-owned capability and to reduce recurrence, avoidable rework, and repeated governance reconstruction.

Result semantics use mandatory outcome gates for functional correctness, quality, safety/security/compliance, verification evidence, and prohibited side effects; failure of a mandatory gate cannot be averaged away by better performance on another dimension.

Beyond mandatory gates, SAGE preserves a provenance-backed multidimensional outcome vector against human-owned intent, requirements, constraints, and Definition of Done, including attainment, correctness/quality, reliability, time, human effort, cost, rework, recurrence, automation leverage, maintainability, stakeholder value, architectural fitness, and improvement opportunity where applicable.

A scalar fitness/utility score is used only when comparison or optimization requires it; its semantics, normalization, tradeoffs, and weights are explicitly human-owned and approved, SAGE/LLM may propose but may not invent the value function, and the underlying vector components and provenance remain available.

Anti-gaming controls prevent SAGE, an LLM, or an implementation from redefining success around convenient metrics, silently changing weights or gates, or substituting proxy optimization for the human-owned Definition of Done.

The metamodel is reconciled with the existing SAGE operating contract, workflow primitives, continuous-improvement model, evidence model, observability model, SAGE-ACTION-20260810-001, and SAGE-ACTION-20260809-002 without absorbing those actions' narrower implementation scopes.

An external-framework review is documented and published using authoritative current sources, covering relevant AWS, Microsoft Azure, IBM, Google Cloud, and NIST governance/architecture guidance; alignment is characterized as comparison, not certification or endorsement, and SAGE-specific extensions are explicitly identified.

Deterministic positive and negative regressions prove shared-responsibility authority boundaries, LLM non-authority, architect break-glass accountability, evidence-backed context disposition, mandatory-gate behavior, outcome-vector preservation, and human-owned scalar semantics.

No orchestration implementation product is selected by this action; BPMN, workflow engines, graph engines/databases, or other products remain later capability-selection decisions governed by measured requirements and evidence.
measurement_plan: Track activity-level responsibility assignments and authority boundaries, including Accountable Owner, Responsible, Contributor, Authority-Approver, and optional Informed roles, and record ambiguous or conflicting assignments as defects.

Track Architect interventions and break-glass events by trigger, rationale, minimum governed scope, controls or assumptions overridden, resulting risk, post-verification result, recurrence class, and whether the class becomes reusable capability.

Track LLM contributions by contribution type (external knowledge, alternatives, critique/risk, verification idea, candidate change), provenance, corroboration outcome, and whether any attempted use crossed a human-reserved or deterministic authority boundary.

Track inferred-context dispositions by applicable-now, conceptually-applicable-but-not-currently-instrumented, capability-gap, and demonstrably-not-applicable, with zero suppressions lacking evidence-backed disposition.

Track deterministic workflow decisions, transitions, retries, compensation, and continuations versus manual reconstruction, including failure recurrence, avoidable rework, and time to validated continuation.

Track workflow/decision observability coverage separately from infrastructure/application observability and measure missing instrumentation, human intervention, process friction, decision latency, and verification evidence availability.

For each governed outcome, record mandatory gate results independently and preserve the applicable multidimensional outcome vector with provenance; require zero cases where a failed mandatory gate is masked by aggregation.

Where a scalar fitness/utility score is used, record the human-approved value-function semantics, normalization, weights, tradeoffs, approval provenance, component vector, and sensitivity to changed assumptions; otherwise preserve scalar neutrality.

Measure effectiveness, efficiency, correctness/quality, reliability, time to validated outcome, human effort, cost, rework, recurrence, automation leverage, maintainability, stakeholder value, architectural fitness, prediction calibration, reuse, and improvement opportunity where the dimensions are applicable and observable.

Measure whether verified interventions, workflow outcomes, evidence use, failures, and repeated patterns are converted into reusable repository-owned capabilities that reduce recurrence, manual correction, governance reconstruction, and avoidable rework.

Record the external-framework review scope, authoritative source provenance, comparison date, identified alignments, deliberate SAGE-specific extensions, and unresolved gaps without treating comparison as certification or endorsement.

actions.title: Add least-authority GitHub inspection capability
actions.desired_outcome: SAGE has a reusable repository-owned least-authority GitHub inspection capability that lets governed workflows independently read and verify pull-request and repository-hosting state without granting those workflows GitHub mutation authority. The capability provides structured, machine-readable facts needed by checkpoint promotion and future workflows, while pull-request creation, merge, comments, labels, branch changes, and other GitHub mutations remain explicit operator.git-proposal boundaries. Generated workflow payloads consume the read-only capability through a stable interface and do not invoke gh or GitHub APIs directly.
acceptance_criteria: A versioned repository-owned GitHub inspection capability exposes only read operations required by governed workflows and is registered through the existing workflow-primitives and capability-selection contracts.

The inspection interface returns structured machine-readable facts sufficient to identify a pull request and verify its base branch, head branch, head SHA, state, merge status, and other explicitly required promotion facts without parsing free-form operator output.
Checkpoint promotion can independently verify the result of an operator-executed pull-request-create boundary using the read-only GitHub inspection capability.

Checkpoint promotion can independently verify the result of an operator-executed pull-request-merge boundary using the read-only GitHub inspection capability, while final source-head containment in origin/main remains a Git read-authority check.
The capability cannot create, merge, close, reopen, comment on, label, approve, edit, or otherwise mutate a pull request, branch, repository, workflow run, release, issue, or other GitHub object.

Generated repository mutation payloads and ordinary workflow compositions are prohibited from invoking gh or GitHub HTTP APIs directly; they must consume the repository-owned inspection interface for reads and operator.git-proposal for mutations.

Any implementation-specific GitHub transport such as gh or an API client is encapsulated behind the trusted least-authority inspection primitive and is not exposed as general command authority to generated workflows.

Authentication or transport failure, ambiguous pull-request identity, mismatched base/head identity, missing expected SHA, or unverifiable merge state fails closed with a structured diagnosis rather than falling back to operator assertion.
The existing Git safety and GitHub mutation guardrails remain at least as strict as before this capability; no broad exception is added for generated helpers or workflow payloads.

Deterministic positive regressions verify read-only PR inspection for pre-merge and post-merge states, and deterministic negative regressions prove mutation attempts and direct gh/API use from generated workflows are rejected.

SAGE-ACTION-20260809-002 checkpoint promotion is updated only to consume the new read-only inspection capability and existing git.inspect/operator.git-proposal roles; it does not gain direct Git or GitHub mutation authority.

The generated-payload validation path invokes the canonical safety analysis early enough that a proposal containing the previously observed MIXED-GIT-AUTHORITY, GIT-MUTATION-API, or direct GITHUB-MUTATION patterns is rejected before request execution.
measurement_plan: Track governed GitHub inspection calls by workflow, requested fact set, result, and failure disposition.
Track checkpoint-promotion PR-create and PR-merge continuations that are independently verified through structured GitHub inspection rather than operator-text interpretation.
Require zero successful GitHub mutations performed through the inspection capability.
Require zero generated workflow payloads accepted with direct gh or GitHub API mutation authority.
Track ambiguous or unverifiable GitHub states that fail closed and whether they lead to reusable capability or contract improvements.
Track recurrence of the checkpoint-promotion Git/GitHub safety failure class after this capability and the associated pre-execution validation regression are implemented.
Measure whether structured GitHub inspection reduces manual verification steps and time from validated checkpoint to safely verified promotion.

history.reason: Register the missing least-authority GitHub inspection capability exposed by repeated checkpoint-promotion safety failures, while preserving operator.git-proposal as the exclusive PR mutation boundary.

Current SAGE discovery, evidence retrieval, and complete baseline validation confirm a real workflow-composition capability gap: governed workflows need structured read-only GitHub pull-request inspection while operator.git-proposal remains the exclusive PR mutation boundary and existing Git/GitHub safety guardrails remain unchanged.

actions.title: Add SAGE semantic understanding, feasibility, and Architect confirmation composition
actions.desired_outcome: SAGE bears the burden of understanding human intent and governed SAGE artifacts while the human Architect retains authority over meaning. SAGE derives an explicit interpretation of the intended problem from human-stated intent and constraints, governed SAGE artifacts and registered workflow semantics, Kalaxy3 accumulated local evidence and experience, deterministic current-state facts, and LLM-contributed external engineering knowledge and alternatives. SAGE must preserve the provenance and epistemic role of those sources rather than flattening them into an undifferentiated experience dump. Before a materially interpreted intent becomes authoritative input to planning or execution, SAGE conducts a governed intent-definition and negotiation interaction. SAGE presents the interpreted intent, proposed scope, requirements, constraints, assumptions, alternatives, best-practice KPI/SLO/SLA and observability suggestions, capability gaps, indirect enabling changes, material ambiguities, tradeoffs, and their provenance. The Architect may accept, reject, modify, or defer those proposals before confirming the resulting intent and scope. During that negotiation, SAGE also evaluates the proposed intent and scope against established SAGE guardrails, metamodel constraints, participant responsibilities, authority boundaries, and trust boundaries. Any conflict is surfaced explicitly before semantic confirmation. If the Architect proposes to proceed despite a permitted conflict, SAGE requires an evidence-backed exception decision that records the governing authority, rationale, affected controls, scope, blast radius, residual risk, compensating controls, and reconciliation and verification obligations. Such an exception is bounded and attributable, travels with downstream planning and execution, does not silently redefine the metamodel or become precedent, and cannot override nondelegable legal, security, compliance, or other mandatory constraints. The negotiated dispositions and rationale are preserved as decision evidence. Semantic confirmation then establishes that SAGE understood the Architect-approved definition and scope of the intended problem; it does not establish that the proposed outcome is logically, technically, operationally, economically, or otherwise feasible. After meaning is confirmed, SAGE performs an explicit feasibility and consistency assessment using quantitative observability and other authoritative current-state evidence across the relevant system, together with deterministic checks, repository authority, available capabilities, governed constraints, and corroborated engineering knowledge. Observability is not limited to infrastructure telemetry: it provides the measurable facts needed to determine whether the intended outcome is achievable under actual resource, behavioral, workflow, dependency, performance, capacity, timing, and platform conditions. SAGE must also use applicable engineering knowledge, including LLM-contributed current best practices, to identify the KPIs, SLOs, SLAs, outcome measures, and other observability signals that should exist for the intended outcome. If current observability cannot measure a material success, feasibility, quality, efficiency, reliability, or constraint dimension, SAGE treats that as a capability gap and may require an observability enhancement as an enabling or prerequisite change before the original architectural intent can be responsibly planned, verified, or declared successful. Claims that can be proven deterministically must be proven before executable planning; claims supported only by evidence must remain evidence-qualified; unresolved uncertainty must remain explicit. Infeasible or insufficiently supported outcomes produce explainable gaps, violated constraints, or feasible alternatives rather than an executable plan. Authorization to mutate remains a separate governed decision after confirmed meaning and adequate feasibility. Material ambiguity produces an Architect clarification boundary rather than silent inference or vocabulary-dependent UNCLASSIFIED failure. Later evidence that materially changes either the confirmed interpretation or feasibility assessment invalidates the affected downstream state and returns SAGE to the appropriate confirmation or feasibility boundary. The composition reuses the implemented repository-owned request-planning capability from SAGE-ACTION-20260808-001 and existing canonical lifecycle, authority, evidence, capability-selection, validation, and deterministic-execution primitives rather than duplicating them. The resulting metamodel, lifecycle semantics, participant responsibilities, intent-negotiation behavior, semantic-confirmation boundary, feasibility model, observability-derived capability-gap behavior, exception handling, authority distinctions, and evidence/provenance model are documented for external consumption in implementation-neutral language. External documentation explains both the normal path and important negative paths, including ambiguity, infeasibility, rejected or deferred proposals, guardrail conflicts, exceptions, and re-entry when later evidence changes meaning or feasibility. Repository-internal schemas and primitives remain traceable implementation evidence, but external readers are not required to understand them in order to understand SAGE's architecture, responsibilities, controls, or value.
acceptance_criteria: SAGE defines a governed semantic-understanding stage whose inputs can include human intent, governed SAGE artifacts, registered workflow identity, repository authority, applicable evidence/experience, deterministic current-state facts, and LLM-contributed external engineering knowledge.

Every interpreted-intent record distinguishes the provenance and epistemic role of human-stated intent, Kalaxy3 local evidence/experience, deterministic current facts, registered workflow or artifact semantics, and LLM-generated external knowledge, alternatives, or inference.

Registered workflows and governed artifact types seed their known semantic contexts deterministically; requesters are not required to know SAGE match terms, schema names, primitive identifiers, or planning-package formats.

SAGE derives an explicit interpreted-intent record containing the intended problem, proposed scope, understood requirements and constraints, material assumptions, relevant alternatives, unresolved gaps or ambiguities, applicable contexts, and evidence provenance.
The interpreted-intent record distinguishes source-stated facts from SAGE inference, generalization, narrowing, and alternative generation so the Architect can see where translation occurred.

Before materially interpreted intent becomes authoritative input to downstream planning or execution, SAGE presents that interpretation to the human Architect for explicit semantic confirmation or correction.

Semantic confirmation means that the Architect agrees SAGE has understood the intended problem and acceptable interpretation; it does not establish feasibility and remains distinct from authority approval to execute.

Before semantic confirmation, SAGE supports a governed intent-definition and negotiation phase in which proposed scope elements, requirements, constraints, alternatives, best-practice recommendations, observability needs, capability gaps, and indirect enabling changes can each be accepted, rejected, modified, or deferred by the Architect.

During intent interpretation and negotiation, SAGE evaluates the proposed intent, scope, participant assignments, authority use, and implementation implications against established SAGE guardrails, metamodel constraints, participant responsibilities, and trust boundaries.

A detected conflict with an established guardrail or metamodel rule is surfaced to the Architect before semantic confirmation with the specific rule or control, why the proposed intent conflicts, the affected participant or authority boundary, and the likely consequence of proceeding.

SAGE distinguishes hard nondelegable constraints from governable exception candidates. Legal, security, compliance, or other explicitly nondelegable constraints cannot be overridden by an Architect exception.

A governable exception can proceed only through an explicit evidence-backed exception decision that records the approving authority, rationale, affected controls, bounded scope, expected duration or termination condition when applicable, blast radius, residual risk, compensating controls, required verification, and reconciliation or rollback obligations.

Exception evidence is bound to the confirmed intent and propagated into downstream feasibility, planning, execution, observability, validation, and closeout so later stages can enforce the approved deviation and its containment requirements.

An exception does not silently amend the SAGE metamodel, guardrail baseline, participant responsibilities, or future default behavior; reuse as precedent requires a separate governed reconciliation or metamodel-change decision.

If downstream evidence shows that an approved exception has exceeded its authorized scope, blast radius, duration, or risk assumptions, SAGE fails closed at the appropriate boundary and returns to Architect/governance review before continuation.

Intent-negotiation dispositions are recorded with provenance, rationale when supplied or required, the proposing source, and the resulting effect on scope, requirements, feasibility obligations, Definition of Done, and downstream planning.

Rejected or deferred SAGE proposals remain available as decision evidence for later analysis and learning but do not silently become authoritative requirements, constraints, precedent, or future defaults.
Accepted negotiation outcomes become part of the Architect-confirmed intent contract and are the semantic basis for subsequent feasibility analysis, planning, validation, and outcome measurement.

SAGE may revisit a previously rejected or deferred proposal only when materially new evidence, changed conditions, or changed intent makes it relevant again; the prior disposition and new basis must both be presented rather than silently overriding the earlier decision.
After semantic confirmation, SAGE performs an explicit feasibility and consistency assessment before producing an executable plan.

Feasibility assessment uses quantitative observability and authoritative current-state evidence to test all applicable operational constraints, including but not limited to storage capacity and retention behavior, CPU/vCPU and memory capacity, network and I/O limits, throughput and latency, quotas, scheduling and placement, dependency state, controller or platform semantics, ordering/FIFO capabilities, timing guarantees, scaling behavior, failure modes, and other measurable conditions relevant to the intended outcome.

SAGE distinguishes measured or observable system constraints from human-owned requirements, policy, legal, security, compliance, budget, and architectural constraints. Both constrain feasibility, but their provenance and authority are preserved rather than collapsed into one generic constraint set.

A feasibility conclusion must identify which constraints were actually observed or deterministically established, which were supplied by governed human or policy authority, which remain assumptions, and which could not yet be measured.

SAGE uses applicable repository evidence and LLM-contributed engineering knowledge to identify fit-for-purpose KPIs, SLOs, SLAs, outcome measures, constraint measurements, and observability signals needed to evaluate the intended outcome; these recommendations remain proposals until reconciled against human intent, repository authority, applicability, and deterministic validation.

When current observability lacks a material measurement required to establish feasibility, verify a mandatory outcome gate, measure effectiveness or efficiency, or determine whether the intended result remains within acceptable operating bounds, SAGE records an explicit observability capability gap rather than treating the unmeasured condition as satisfied.

An observability capability gap discovered while pursuing another architectural intent may become an enabling prerequisite or derived improvement action. SAGE preserves the causal relationship to the originating intent so the indirect change is justified as necessary to understand, validate, or operate the requested outcome rather than as unrelated scope expansion.

SAGE distinguishes observability required before execution to establish feasibility from observability required during or after execution to verify outcome attainment, SLO/SLA compliance, efficiency, reliability, quality, friction, and learning.

SAGE may recommend changes to existing KPIs, SLOs, SLAs, dashboards, telemetry, workflow measurements, or evidence capture when current measures are insufficient or misaligned with the Architect-confirmed intent, but material changes to human-owned service objectives, acceptance thresholds, or business commitments require the appropriate human authority.

Where deterministic proof is not possible, SAGE records evidence-supported claims, assumptions, confidence or uncertainty, and corroboration separately from proven facts rather than presenting them as certainty.
Prior Kalaxy3 experience may establish precedent or a known implementation pattern but cannot by itself establish that the same outcome is feasible under the current facts and constraints.

LLM-generated engineering knowledge or alternatives may contribute to interpretation and feasibility analysis but cannot independently establish deterministic feasibility, authority, or successful execution.

An outcome that is understood correctly but fails feasibility or consistency checks produces explicit violated constraints, missing capabilities, evidence gaps, or feasible alternatives and cannot silently proceed into executable planning.

Meaning, feasibility, and authorization are represented as separate governed assertions with distinct provenance and status: the Architect validates meaning, SAGE plus deterministic verification establish feasibility to the degree supportable, and governance determines authorization.
The same human interaction may satisfy semantic confirmation and subsequent authority approval when policy permits, but evidence preserves the distinct decisions and their meanings.

Material ambiguity, conflicting interpretations, materially different viable scopes, or insufficient information produces an Architect clarification boundary rather than silent selection or vocabulary-dependent UNCLASSIFIED failure.

Non-material inferences may proceed without interrupting the Architect only when their basis and provenance are recorded and they cannot materially alter outcome, requirements, constraints, authority, mutation scope, Definition of Done, risk, feasibility, or architectural fitness.
If later evidence materially changes the confirmed interpretation, SAGE invalidates the affected semantic confirmation and returns to the semantic-confirmation boundary before continuing.

If later evidence materially changes feasibility without changing meaning, SAGE invalidates the affected feasibility result and repeats feasibility assessment without unnecessarily asking the Architect to reconfirm unchanged intent.

Accepted improvement-action contracts can serve as governed semantic inputs to request planning without requiring the Architect or an external helper to manually construct sage-source.json or reconstruct SAGE-owned planning semantics.
The composition reuses SAGE-ACTION-20260808-001 for downstream capability derivation, candidate selection, and capability-gap handling rather than reimplementing request-planning behavior.

Canonical action-ID allocation, lifecycle registration, evidence retrieval, authority reconciliation, component selection, capability-gap handling, Git inspection, operator mutation boundaries, validation, and continuation are reused through existing repository-owned contracts.

SAGE can derive a proposed improvement-action draft from interpreted and confirmed semantics and present that draft for human meaning validation before canonical registration; the human is not required to author the internal improvement-action representation.

Positive regressions prove semantically equivalent requests classify and plan without canonical vocabulary, accepted actions seed planning semantics directly, confirmed meaning enters feasibility assessment, and feasible results enter the existing deterministic planner without caller-authored internal schemas.

Negative regressions prove materially ambiguous requests stop at clarification, incorrect interpretations can be corrected before planning, unconfirmed material interpretations cannot proceed, semantically correct but infeasible outcomes are blocked, unsupported feasibility claims are not promoted to certainty, and later material evidence invalidates stale confirmation or feasibility state as appropriate.

A regression reproduces the observed lifecycle-acceptance failure in which a legitimate improvement-action transition was UNCLASSIFIED until the requester supplied internal terms such as 'improvement action' and 'action lifecycle', and proves registered workflow semantics eliminate that vocabulary dependency.

A regression reproduces the observed request-planning gap in which production planning accepted only a caller-constructed sage-source.json package, and proves a governed accepted action can reach the existing planning composition without requiring Architect-authored planning internals.
A feasibility regression demonstrates that a known-good Kalaxy3 implementation pattern is rejected or adapted when current deterministic facts violate its assumptions or constraints.
The composition remains implementation-neutral with respect to orchestration engines, BPMN, graph technologies, agent frameworks, or user-interface mechanisms.

The SAGE external documentation describes the complete intent-to-outcome lifecycle in implementation-neutral language, including intent interpretation, expert proposals, Architect negotiation, semantic confirmation, feasibility assessment, authorization, deterministic execution, measurement, learning, and re-entry when material evidence changes prior conclusions.

External documentation explains the four participant classes and their contribution, accountability, authority, and trust-boundary distinctions, including why the LLM may contribute broad engineering knowledge without holding deterministic or human-reserved authority.
External documentation explains the distinction among meaning, feasibility, and authorization, including which participant or control is responsible for each assertion.

External documentation explains how Kalaxy3 experience, deterministic current facts, human intent, registered workflow/artifact semantics, and LLM-contributed engineering knowledge are reconciled and how provenance is preserved.

External documentation explains the governed intent-negotiation model, including accept, reject, modify, and defer dispositions and how those decisions become reusable evidence without silently becoming future requirements or precedent.

External documentation explains how observability supports feasibility and outcome measurement, how SAGE can identify missing KPIs/SLOs/SLAs or other measurements, and how an observability capability gap may become an enabling prerequisite derived from another architectural intent.

External documentation explains guardrail and metamodel compatibility checks, governable exceptions, nondelegable constraints, exception evidence, bounded scope and blast radius, compensating controls, downstream propagation, and why an exception does not automatically amend the governing metamodel.

External documentation includes at least one end-to-end worked example showing an Architect request evolving through interpretation, negotiation, observability or feasibility findings, confirmation, authorization, execution planning, and evidence capture.

External documentation includes at least one negative-path example showing a correctly understood but infeasible intent and at least one example showing a requested intent that conflicts with an established SAGE guardrail or participant-authority boundary.

Documentation clearly separates normative SAGE architectural contracts from illustrative implementation details so external reviewers can assess the metamodel without assuming a specific workflow engine, BPMN implementation, graph technology, agent framework, or repository layout.
Published documentation links architectural claims to repository evidence, validated examples, relevant standards, and current external framework comparisons with provenance and review dates.
External documentation is included in the Definition of Done and cannot be considered complete merely because repository code and internal contracts have been implemented.

Track first-pass semantic confirmation rate and Architect corrections, distinguishing SAGE misunderstanding from legitimate changes in human intent.

actions.title: Make governed candidate iteration first-class
actions.desired_outcome: SAGE treats engineering delivery as one governed objective with an evolving candidate implementation and durable non-promotable checkpoints rather than as repeated objective-fail/restart cycles. Intent-to-outcome owns candidate iteration and re-entry semantics, request planning converts Architect-confirmed semantic effects into domain-level planning obligations, existing Kalaxy3 capabilities are reused before new components are proposed, and unresolved domain requirements produce explicit capability-gap evidence. The current zero-trust iteration at commit 4db88558aff3c7f973b129e63b5a5c6cde55a4a7 is the deterministic starting case: the negotiated secrets-management requirement must survive into planning, Ansible remains the established deployment/control model, Terraform is not introduced, and intermediate checkpoints remain non-promotable until the complete applicable outcome gate passes.
acceptance_criteria: The active objective and Architect-confirmed intent remain distinct from mutable candidate implementations, durable non-promotable checkpoints, and promotion.
The current candidate at commit 4db88558aff3c7f973b129e63b5a5c6cde55a4a7 is preserved as iteration 1 without claiming that the objective is complete or promotable.

The repository-owned intent-to-outcome lifecycle records candidate iteration identity, parent checkpoint, triggering observation, affected requirements or planning obligations, validation state, unresolved findings, learning, invalidated downstream state, and the next governed boundary.
Implementation-local refinement continues from the current candidate without restarting the objective, semantic discovery, planning, or evidence retrieval when governing conditions are unchanged.

A material change to meaning, authority, scope, required capability, safety or trust boundary, or another governing condition invalidates only affected downstream state and re-enters the earliest necessary governed boundary.

actions.title: Portable Stage Execution, Artifact Promotion, Engine-Neutral Orchestration, and Constraint-Aware Governed Phasing
actions.desired_outcome: Deliver a demonstrable SAGE delivery architecture in which Git/PR can invoke a portable multi-architecture canonical stage independent of the operator device; stage builds/tests/generates once and emits immutable artifacts and evidence; promotion binds only target-environment affinity and deploys already-proven artifacts; execution hosts and workflow engines remain replaceable; convergence consumes applicable check evidence; evidence invalidation re-enters only the earliest materially affected domain; completed child promotion reconciles into parent intent lineage; and real-world immutable constraints can change scope/phasing only through explicit, traceable Architect disposition that preserves quality, security, intent, evidence, learning, innovation, and reconciliation obligations.
acceptance_criteria: The four-role SAGE architecture and existing intent lifecycle remain authoritative; CI/CD engines, OCI executors, runners, and environment manifests do not acquire Architect or semantic authority.
A versioned multi-architecture OCI stage contract can be invoked from Git/PR without requiring the end-user workstation to define or build the stage environment.
Stage builds/tests/generates once and produces immutable artifact digests, provenance, and stage evidence that production promotion consumes without rebuilding absent an explicit governed reason.

Execution hosts and workflow engines are replaceable implementations; GitHub Actions, Jenkins, self-hosted runners, dedicated builders, or Kubernetes may invoke the same engine-neutral stage/promotion contract.

Environment manifests bind only target-specific configuration, secret authority, artifact selection, topology/placement, routing/DNS/Access, deployment, observability/runtime verification, and receipts.

Stage, controller qualification, promotion, and runtime evidence are distinct domains; changes invalidate only the earliest materially affected domain instead of invalidating runtime solely because HEAD changed.

actions.title: Make fail-closed recovery self-directing and recurrence-aware
actions.desired_outcome: SAGE owns recovery from every fail-closed state. It persists stable failure and governing-condition identities across attempts, distinguishes a genuinely new governance change from one already consumed by an earlier required re-entry, recognizes unchanged recurrence, prevents repeated identical governance loops, and emits exactly one machine-readable governed next boundary. When the current lifecycle has no authorized transition, including live failure of an accepted control, SAGE emits the capability-gap/successor-action route itself instead of requiring the LLM or operator to inspect repository source and invent recovery.
acceptance_criteria: Every fail-closed closeout contains one structured next-boundary decision or an explicit terminal/no-action decision.
Failure identity persists across attempts using stable request, component, failure-signature, and repository-authority evidence with previous-failure references.
The second live Action-002 ancestry failure at HEAD 4192551f1df150d06d8ad62235746bc5f29eaa18 is deterministically classified as recurrence rather than classification=new.
A governing-condition change has a stable fingerprint and is marked consumed by the re-entry it required; the unchanged fingerprint is not reported as newly changed on the next attempt.
The exact live Action-002 sequence cannot route to planning twice for the same repository-owned-composition fingerprint at unchanged authority.
An unchanged recurrence routes to the owning repair/regression/revalidation boundary rather than repeating discovery or planning.

If the owning control is already accepted and cannot be amended under lifecycle policy, SAGE emits a verified successor capability-gap/improvement-action boundary without LLM/operator source-code inspection.
The emitted boundary identifies owning component, reason, required evidence, mutation authority, and exactly one repository-owned operator command or explicit Architect decision boundary.

The false origin/main ancestry assertion has a deterministic regression proving request execution does not require current remote main to be an ancestor of an otherwise synchronized governed feature HEAD unless an applicable authority explicitly requires it.
Request execution, intent-to-outcome, failure diagnosis, post-retrieval continuation, and action lifecycle consume one recovery identity/next-boundary contract instead of divergent local classifiers.
Repeated discovery, retrieval, semantic confirmation, or planning with no new governing-condition fingerprint fails closed as over-governance before another mutation.
Positive and negative regressions prove: new governance change -> earliest required re-entry once; unchanged recurrence -> repair; exhausted/unsupported recovery -> successor gap/action.
Structured events and closeouts make recurrence, consumed changes, prevented loops, operator boundaries, and avoidable rework measurable.
